questionText:
An audit of a banking transactions system has found that on an earlier occasion, two joint holders of account $A$ attempted simultaneous transfers of Rs. 10000 each from account $A$ to account $B$. Both transactions read the same value, Rs. 11000, as the initial balance in $A$ and were allowed to go through. $B$ was credited Rs. 10000 twice. $A$ was debited only once and ended up with a balance of Rs. 1000.

Which of the following properties is/are certain to have been violated by the system?
explanation:
Step-by-step Explanation:

1. Analysis of the Scenario:
• Initial balance of $A$ = Rs. 11,000.
• Two concurrent transactions $T_1$ and $T_2$ both attempt to transfer Rs. 10,000 from $A$ to $B$.
• Both $T_1$ and $T_2$ read $A = 11000$ simultaneously (a classic lost update / concurrency issue).
• $T_1$ debits $A$ by 10,000 and writes $A = 1000$, and credits $B$ by 10,000.
• $T_2$ also debits $A$ by 10,000 based on its initial read of 11,000, overwriting $A = 1000$, and credits $B$ by 10,000.
• Result: Account $B$ received Rs. 20,000 while account $A$ was reduced by only Rs. 10,000.

2. Evaluating ACID Properties:
• Isolation (Violated): Concurrent execution led to an un-isolated lost update phenomenon where $T_2$ overwrote $T_1$'s update without being isolated from it.
• Consistency (Violated): The total amount of money in the system changed incorrectly (Rs. 10,000 created artificially), violating the integrity constraints/invariants of a bank system.
• Atomicity (Not Violated): All operations within both transactions executed completely (all-or-nothing held).
• Durability (Not Violated): The completed transactions successfully persisted in the database.

Hence, the properties violated are Consistency and Isolation, corresponding to Options (B) and (C).
